scope: DSA and DBMS technical questions, including marked adjacent structural questions. AI search questions are classified separately rather than counted as additional DSA evidence.

families.subject: dsa
families.title: Python objects, scope and simultaneous updates
families.concept: A program’s output follows object identity and the actual order of evaluation, not what an operation sounds like.
reasoningSteps: Draw separate objects and name-to-object arrows.
Evaluate all right-hand sides before a multiple assignment.
Mark mutations separately from rebinding.
Carry persistent defaults or closure state across calls.
commonFailures: Treating append like extend
Assuming a default list is recreated per call
Updating tuple-assignment variables one at a time
families.workedExample: With a=[1]; b=a; a=a+[2], the concatenation creates a new list. Therefore a is [1,2], b remains [1]. Replacing the last statement by a.append(2) would mutate the shared object, making both names see [1,2].

problems.prompt: a=[2]; b=a; c=a[:]; b.append(5). Give a,b,c and identify the shared object.
problems.answer: a=b=[2,5], c=[2]. a and b name one list; c names a copy.

problems.prompt: Start a=[1]. Compare a.append([2,3]) with a.extend([2,3]), each on a fresh a.
problems.answer: Append gives [1,[2,3]]; extend gives [1,2,3].

problems.prompt: def collect(v,L=[]): L.append(v); return L. Three separate print calls evaluate collect(4), collect(7), collect(9,[]). Give each printed line.
problems.answer: [4]; [4,7]; [9]. The explicit empty list is a new argument; the default object persists across the first two calls.

problems.prompt: A={1,2}; B={2,3}; C={2,3,4}; execute A,B,C=A-B,B-C,C-A. Give the three results. Compare with executing those three assignments sequentially.
problems.answer: Simultaneous: A={1}, B=∅, C={3,4}, because all right sides use the old sets. Sequentially: A={1}, B=∅, C={2,3,4}; the final difference uses the updated A and therefore retains2.

problems.prompt:
def factory():
    x=[]
    def add(v):
        x.append(v)
        return x[:]
    return add
f=factory(); g=factory()
p=f(2); q=f(6); r=g(8)
Give p,q,r. Explain both shared closure state and snapshot copying.
problems.answer: p=[2], q=[2,6], r=[8]. Calls through f share one captured list; g captures another. Returning x[:] produces independent snapshots.

teachingSections.title: A name points to an object
teachingSections.text: Think of a Python list as a container holding values. A variable such as a is a name that points to that container. The statement b=a gives the same container another name. It does not copy the contents. If an operation changes the container, both names see that change.

teachingSections.title: Changing a list and replacing a name are different actions
teachingSections.text: Start with a=[1] and b=a. The statement a.append(2) changes the shared list, so both names now see [1,2]. Start again. The statement a=a+[2] first creates a new list. It then makes a point to the new list. The name b still points to the old [1]. Draw two containers to check this.

teachingSections.title: Some objects survive between calls
teachingSections.text: A default list in a function definition is created when Python defines the function. Later calls that omit that argument use the same list. A list created inside a function is different: each execution creates a new one. When an inner function continues to use an outer function’s list, it keeps a reference to that list. This is called a closure. Two separate calls to the outer function create separate lists.

teachingSections.title: Follow the actual sequence of events
teachingSections.text: In a multiple assignment such as a,b=b,a, Python evaluates the right side before changing either name. The result is a swap. For exam code, keep a table of the names, the objects they refer to, and the contents after each statement. Explain each change before predicting the printed output.

families.subject: dsa
families.title: Stacks, queues and evolving control state
prerequisites: Difference between removed values and remaining state
families.concept: A container trace is a state machine: control variables and container contents jointly determine the next operation.
reasoningSteps: Choose a top/front convention.
Record state before and after each operation.
Update flags immediately.
Record popped values separately from the remaining container.
commonFailures: Ignoring a flag change within the same loop iteration
Adding an extra popped value to an accumulator
Reversing front and back
families.workedExample: Push 2, push 5, pop into x, then push x+1 gives stack [2,6] with top at the right. The removed value is 5; it is not still in the stack.

problems.prompt: Apply push(3),push(8),pop to an empty stack; apply enqueue(3),enqueue(8),dequeue to an empty queue. Give removed values and final contents.
problems.answer: Stack removes 8 and leaves [3]. Queue removes 3 and leaves [8].

problems.prompt: A deque starts empty. insertLast(2), insertFirst(7), insertLast(9), removeFirst(), removeLast(). List both removed values and final deque.
problems.answer: The removals are 7 then 9; final deque [2].

problems.prompt: A stack contains [0,1,2,3,4] with top right. Repeatedly pop x; if x is odd and the stack is nonempty, pop one more value but do not add that extra value. Add x to a running total. Give the total and trace.
problems.answer: Pop 4: total4. Pop3, discard2: total7. Pop1, discard0: total8. Final total8.

problems.prompt: Repeat the previous control rule for stack [0,1,2,3,4,5]. What changes?
problems.answer: Pop5 discard4, pop3 discard2, pop1 discard0. Total9.

problems.prompt: A queue starts [1,2,3] with front left. Repeat exactly three times: remove front x, append x+2, and add x to total. Give the total and final queue.
problems.answer: Removed 1,2,3, total6; final queue [3,4,5]. A stack interpretation would produce a different sequence.

teachingSections.title: Choose the end from which values leave
teachingSections.text: A stack removes the most recently added value. This rule is called last in, first out, or LIFO. A queue removes the value that has waited longest. This is first in, first out, or FIFO. In our drawings, a stack’s top is on the right. A queue’s front is on the left.

teachingSections.title: Separate the operation from its result
teachingSections.text: Suppose a stack contains [2,5]. Popping it removes 5 and leaves [2]. If the program stores that removed value in x, then x is 5. The container and the returned value are two different parts of the program’s state. A later statement can change either one.

teachingSections.title: A deque lets you use both ends
teachingSections.text: A double-ended queue, or deque, supports insertion and removal at either end. Draw the full list after each operation. Label the left end as front and the right end as rear. Read removeFirst as an instruction to remove the current front, even if an earlier insertion changed which value is there.

teachingSections.title: Control variables decide what happens next
teachingSections.text: A flag is an ordinary variable used to select between behaviors. If a statement changes the flag, later if statements in that same loop iteration see the new value. Trace a loop with columns for the container, the removed value, the flag and the running total. This makes an extra pop visible even when its value is discarded.

families.subject: dsa
families.title: Recursion: outputs, call counts and cost models
prerequisites: Total calls versus maximum active depth
families.concept: A recurrence must count the exact quantity asked for; output value, total calls, depth and expected work are different objects.
reasoningSteps: Name the counted primitive.
Expand a tiny call tree including base-case calls.
Separate sequential branches from simultaneous stack depth.
For expected cost, average over the stated random choice.
commonFailures: Replacing an expected pivot split by a balanced split
Counting only non-base calls
Reporting depth when asked for total activations
families.workedExample: If F(n) calls F(n−1) and F(n−2) for n>0 and stops for n≤0, total activations obey C(n)=1+C(n−1)+C(n−2), with C(0)=C(−1)=1. This differs from the returned value recurrence.

problems.prompt: For that function, list C(0), C(1), C(2), C(3), counting every invocation.
Binary search uses a three-way midpoint comparison, then chooses one half. With at most 15 elements, give its maximum number of midpoint comparisons on an unsuccessful search.
problems.answer: 4: a largest remaining-size sequence is 15→7→3→1→0. Count one comparison for each nonempty interval.

problems.prompt: Quicksort receives a random permutation of n distinct keys and picks the first key as pivot. Write the expected-work recurrence assuming linear partition cost.
problems.answer: T(n)=(1/n)Σ[k=0 to n−1](T(k)+T(n−1−k))+Θ(n). Uniform pivot rank, two recursive subarrays, and partition work must all be represented.

problems.prompt: For n a power of two, compare T(n)=2T(n/2)+n with U(n)=U(n−1)+n, with constant base costs. Explain the sums.
problems.answer: T has log2 n levels with Θ(n) work per level: Θ(n log n). U sums n+(n−1)+…+1: Θ(n²).

problems.prompt: The two-branch function above is evaluated at n=4 without memoization. Give total calls and maximum simultaneously active calls, including the initial and base calls.
problems.answer: C(4)=1+9+5=15 total. A longest chain is 4,3,2,1,0, so maximum active calls=5.

teachingSections.title: A recursive call is another execution of the function
teachingSections.text: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input. Each call has its own local input and must eventually reach a stopping case, called a base case. To understand a new function, start with a small input. Write which calls it makes and what each returns.

teachingSections.title: Decide what the question wants you to count
teachingSections.text: A function’s returned value, its total number of calls and its deepest chain of unfinished calls can all differ. The runtime stack holds unfinished calls. If a question asks for total activations, count every call, including calls that stop immediately. If it asks for maximum stack depth, count the longest chain that exists at one time.

teachingSections.title: Write a recurrence that matches that count
teachingSections.text: A recurrence describes a quantity using the same quantity on smaller inputs. Suppose every non-base call makes two further calls. Its total-call count is one for the current call plus the call counts of both children. A binary-search call follows only one half, so its comparison count uses one smaller subproblem instead of two.

teachingSections.title: Average over the choices that are actually random
teachingSections.text: In quicksort on a random ordering of distinct keys, the first key can have any rank with equal probability. A rank with k smaller keys leaves subarrays of sizes k and n−1−k. Calculate the recursive work for each possible rank. Average those values, then add the work of partitioning. Assuming an equal split would replace the stated random process with a different one.

families.subject: dsa
families.title: Hashing: collision traces and expected-cost assumptions
families.concept: A hash value is a starting location; the collision policy determines the actual position and search path.
reasoningSteps: Calculate the initial hash.
Probe consecutive occupied slots, wrapping modulo capacity.
Maintain the table after every insertion.
Connect insertion to unsuccessful lookup under the stated probabilistic model.
commonFailures: Writing the hash value as the final slot
Ignoring wraparound
Treating an expected bound as a worst-case guarantee
families.workedExample: With capacity7 and h(k)=k mod7, inserting 6,13,20 occupies slots6,0,1. A search for20 must follow that same probe sequence. Deleting13 by simply making slot0 empty would break a search that stops at the first empty slot.

problems.prompt: Compute 18 mod7 and list the probe sequence starting there through four positions.
problems.answer: 4; positions4,5,6,0.

problems.prompt: Capacity7, h(k)=k mod7, linear probing: insert 2,9,16,3. Give final slots.
At load α=0.8, an unsuccessful search has expected probe bound 1/(1−α). Explain why insertion of an absent key has the same search bound, and compute it.
problems.answer: Insertion follows the unsuccessful-search probes to the first empty slot; the bound is5 under the stated uniform-hashing model. It is not a worst-case guarantee.

problems.prompt: In the capacity7 table from the worked example, delete13. Explain the role of a tombstone when looking up20.
problems.answer: Search must continue past the deleted slot0; a tombstone preserves the probe chain. Marking it empty can incorrectly terminate the search.

problems.prompt: Capacity5, h(k)=2k mod5, insert 1,6,11,2. Give slots and say whether the sequence exhibits a collision cluster.
problems.answer: 1→2,6→3,11→4,2→0. Yes: the initial hash for the first three is2, and the cluster wraps for the last insertion.

teachingSections.title: A hash chooses where to start
teachingSections.text: A hash table stores values in numbered positions. A hash function turns a key into a starting position. The expression k mod m means the remainder after dividing k by m. It always gives a position from 0 to m−1. For example, 18 mod7 is4 because18=2×7+4.

teachingSections.title: Collisions need a rule
teachingSections.text: Two keys may have the same starting position. This is a collision. With linear probing, try that position first. If it is occupied, try the next position. Continue until an empty position appears. After the last position, return to position0. Record each insertion before handling the next key.

teachingSections.title: A search must follow the same route
teachingSections.text: To find a key, repeat its insertion route. An empty position normally means the key is absent. Deletion therefore needs care. A tombstone is a marker saying a value was deleted but the search must continue. Replacing a deleted position with an ordinary empty position may hide a later key.

teachingSections.title: An average bound needs assumptions
teachingSections.text: The load factor is the number of stored keys divided by the number of positions. A fuller table tends to require more probes. A bound stated under uniform hashing is an average under that model. It is not a guarantee for every arrangement, and it is not automatically a formula for every linear-probing implementation. Use the assumptions and bound supplied in the question.

families.subject: dsa
families.title: Sorting: implementation traces, passes and inversions
families.concept: Knowing Θ(n²) does not determine exact comparisons, swaps, shifts or the array after a stated number of passes.
reasoningSteps: Write the exact implementation convention.
Trace one pass, counting only the specified comparison.
Connect adjacent swaps with inversion count when applicable.
Test all answer options separately.
commonFailures: Equating comparisons with swaps
Counting a self-swap as necessary
Using an early-exit optimization not stated in the question
families.workedExample: In insertion sort on [1,3,2], comparing3>2 causes one shift; comparing1>2 is false and stops the scan. Counting only key comparisons gives3 overall: one during insertion of3, then two during insertion of2.

problems.prompt: List the inversion pairs in [3,1,2]. What is the minimum number of adjacent swaps needed to sort it?
problems.answer: Pairs (3,1),(3,2); two adjacent swaps.

problems.prompt: Trace the first two outer iterations of insertion sort on [4,2,3,1]. Give the array after each and total element shifts.
Compare fixed-pass bubble sort (n−1 passes, inner lengths n−1,n−2,…,1, no early exit) with standard insertion sort (shift while a[j]>key). On [1,2,4,3], count key comparisons and swaps/shifts.
problems.answer: Bubble:6 comparisons,1 adjacent swap. Insertion:1+1+2=4 key comparisons,1 shift. Do not count index tests.

problems.prompt: Using those exact implementations on [1,2,3,4], give both comparison counts and explain the best-case difference.
problems.answer: Bubble still6; insertion3. A different optimized bubble implementation could stop early, so the code convention matters.

problems.prompt: For [1,3,x,5,4], which x in {2,4,6} yields exactly two adjacent swaps in insertion sort? Give the inversion count for each.
problems.answer: Only x=2. Inversion counts are2,1,3 for x=2,4,6 respectively. Equal4 values do not form an inversion.

teachingSections.title: Choose exactly what you will count
teachingSections.text: Sorting puts values in order. A key comparison asks how two values compare. A swap exchanges two values. A shift copies a value to a neighboring position. These actions have different counts. Write the question’s counting rule above your trace. Unless asked otherwise, keep loop-bound tests separate from comparisons between values.

teachingSections.title: Insertion sort grows an ordered prefix
teachingSections.text: After each insertion-sort iteration, the processed part at the left is sorted. Save the next value as the key. Move larger earlier values one position right until the key can be placed. With the condition earlierValue>key, equal values do not move past one another. This preserves their original order, a property called stability.

teachingSections.title: Bubble sort fixes values at the far end
teachingSections.text: In a left-to-right bubble-sort pass, compare neighboring values and exchange them when they are out of order. The largest value in that pass reaches the right end. A version that always completes every pass can perform more comparisons than a version that stops after a pass with no swaps. State which version you are using before claiming an exact count.

teachingSections.title: Use inversions to explain adjacent swaps
teachingSections.text: An inversion is a pair of positions whose earlier value is larger than the later value. Equal values do not form an inversion. Swapping an out-of-order neighboring pair removes exactly one inversion. Therefore a sorting method using only those swaps needs one swap per original inversion. This explains a count that a long trace might otherwise obscure.

families.subject: dsa
families.title: Trees: reconstructing structure and proving bounds
families.concept: Traversal sequences encode structural constraints; uniqueness requires the right assumptions, not just a memorized pair of traversals.
reasoningSteps: Locate the root using preorder or postorder.
Partition the inorder sequence into left and right subtrees.
Recurse on the corresponding subsequences.
Check each structural claim against the reconstructed tree or a counterexample.
commonFailures: Confusing a binary tree with a BST
Assuming preorder alone determines shape
Applying full-tree equalities to an arbitrary binary tree
families.workedExample: Preorder A,B,D,C with inorder D,B,A,C gives rootA, left subtree rooted atB with left childD, and right childC. Its postorder is D,B,C,A.

problems.prompt: Give preorder, inorder and postorder for rootM with left childL and right childR.
problems.answer: Preorder M,L,R; inorder L,M,R; postorder L,R,M.

problems.prompt: Reconstruct preorder A,B,C,D and inorder B,A,D,C. Give postorder.
problems.answer: RootA; leftB; rightC with leftD. Postorder B,D,C,A.

problems.prompt: Can preorder A,B and postorder B,A uniquely determine an arbitrary binary tree? What if every internal node has exactly two children?
problems.answer: For an arbitrary tree, B can be left or right, so not unique. The two-node case violates the full-tree assumption; for a full binary tree with distinct labels, preorder plus postorder determines structure recursively.

problems.prompt: A rooted full binary tree has 5 internal nodes. Derive its number of leaves and total nodes using edges.
problems.answer: There are2I edges, also I+L−1 edges; L=I+1=6 and N=11.

problems.prompt: With height counted in edges, give minimum and maximum node counts for a binary tree of height3. Exhibit shapes attaining them.
problems.answer: Minimum4: one root-to-leaf chain. Maximum15: a complete tree with all levels0–3 filled. Structural bounds, not a BST ordering fact.

teachingSections.title: A tree records parent and child relationships
teachingSections.text: A rooted tree has a distinguished starting node, called the root. Each other node has one parent. A binary tree permits a left child and a right child at each node. A leaf has no children. A full binary tree requires each non-leaf node to have exactly two children.

teachingSections.title: A traversal chooses when to visit the root
teachingSections.text: Preorder visits the root, then the left subtree, then the right subtree. Inorder visits left subtree, root, right subtree. Postorder visits left subtree, right subtree, root. Apply the same rule again inside every subtree. These are rules about visiting a given tree, not rules that sort its labels.

teachingSections.title: Two sequences can reveal the missing structure
teachingSections.text: Assume labels are distinct. The first preorder label identifies the root. Find that label in inorder. Labels before it belong to the left subtree and labels after it belong to the right subtree. The number of left-subtree labels tells you how to split the remaining preorder sequence. Repeat this process on each smaller part.

teachingSections.title: Read the assumptions before claiming uniqueness
teachingSections.text: Preorder alone leaves the side of a single child unknown. Preorder and postorder can also leave that ambiguity for an arbitrary binary tree. The full-tree assumption removes single-child cases. For counting questions, specify whether height counts edges or nodes. A height-three chain has four nodes when height counts edges.

families.subject: dsa
families.title: Graphs: reachability, discovery order and counterexamples
families.concept: Traversal order, reachable set and shortest-path distance answer different questions. Universal claims need proofs or small counterexamples.
reasoningSteps: Identify whether the question asks for order, a set, or distance.
Write the specified neighbor order before tracing.
Reverse an entire path to reason about a reversed graph.
Disprove a universal claim with the smallest legal graph.
commonFailures: Assuming BFS and DFS have the same visitation order
Using numeric vertex order instead of adjacency order
Checking a necessary constraint as though it were sufficient
families.workedExample: If u reaches v via u→a→v, reversing every edge yields v→a→u. Thus reversing the graph reverses reachability direction. It does not generally reverse a traversal’s discovery list.

problems.prompt: For edges A→B and B→C, list vertices reachable from A in G and from A in the reversed graph, including the starting vertex.
problems.answer: In G: A,B,C. In reversed G: A only.

problems.prompt: Vertices0…6 have edges i→i+1 and i→i+2 when endpoints exist. DFS from0 examines larger neighbors first. Give discovery order.
problems.answer: 0,2,4,6,5,3,1. Track returns from recursion rather than sorting the reachable set.

problems.prompt: Suppose u is visited by DFS from v in G. Which reachability claim is guaranteed in the reversed graph, and why?
problems.answer: BFS from u in the reversed graph reaches v: reverse the original path v→…→u. The traversal algorithm affects order, not the reachable set.

problems.prompt: A known shortest unweighted path is A–B–C–D, of length3. Could A–C be an additional edge? Could A–D? Justify using shorter paths.
problems.answer: Neither: A–C–D would have length2 and A–D length1, contradicting the stated shortest distance.

problems.prompt: A DAG has edges P→Q,R→Q,Q→S,Q→T. Test P,R,Q,T,S and P,Q,R,S,T as topological orders. Give the violating edge for any failure.
problems.answer: First is valid. Second violates R→Q because R appears after Q. This is an adjacent structural extension of the basic graph syllabus; give it lower priority than traversal and shortest paths.

teachingSections.title: An edge describes an allowed step
teachingSections.text: A graph consists of vertices and edges. A directed edge A→B allows a step from A to B. It does not by itself allow a return step. A path is a sequence of allowed steps. Vertex B is reachable from A when some path leads from A to B.

teachingSections.title: Reachable vertices and visit order are different answers
teachingSections.text: Breadth-first search uses a queue and explores increasing distances in an unweighted graph. Depth-first search follows a branch and returns when that branch has no unvisited continuation. Both can find the same reachable vertices. Their discovery orders can differ. DFS order also depends on which neighbor it tries first.

teachingSections.title: Reverse a path one edge at a time
teachingSections.text: Suppose A→B→C is a path. Reversing every edge produces C→B→A. This proves that if A reaches C in the original graph, C reaches A in the reversed graph. The proof does not need a particular visit order. Draw a small example before adding cycles or extra edges.

teachingSections.title: Use a shorter route to reject an impossible edge
teachingSections.text: If A–B–C–D is a shortest path, its length is3. An extra A–C edge would provide A–C–D, of length2. That contradicts the stated shortest distance. For a claim about every graph, try to prove it from a path or find a small counterexample. Keep discovery order, reachability and shortest distance separate while doing so.

families.subject: dbms
families.title: Keys, foreign keys and ER-to-relation modelling
families.concept: Constraints are universal schema rules; examples cannot create extra keys or nullability restrictions absent from the schema.
reasoningSteps: Identify each declared constraint and its table.
Distinguish a referenced primary key from a referencing foreign key.
Construct a legal counterexample to an alleged guarantee.
Map entities, many-to-many relations and multivalued attributes separately.
commonFailures: Calling every foreign key a candidate key
Assuming every column is NOT NULL
Merging a multivalued attribute into a single atomic column
families.workedExample: Person(pid PRIMARY KEY), Purchase(orderid PRIMARY KEY,pid REFERENCES Person) permits several purchases with the same pid. The foreign key requires a referenced parent when non-null; it does not make Purchase.pid unique.

problems.prompt: With that schema, is Purchase.pid necessarily a candidate key? Give a legal instance showing your answer.
problems.answer: No. Person has pid1; Purchase may have (order10,pid1),(order11,pid1).

problems.prompt: Ignoring unrelated constraints, which operations can never newly violate this foreign key: insert a parent, delete a child, delete a parent, insert a child? Explain.
problems.answer: Insert a parent and delete a child. Deleting a referenced parent or inserting an unmatched child can violate it under restrictive referential handling.

problems.prompt: Entities Student(sid,name,phone multivalued) and Course(cid,title) have a many-to-many Enrol relation. Under ordinary atomic relational mapping and no additional FDs, give the minimum relations and their keys.
problems.answer: Student(sid,name), StudentPhone(sid,phone), Course(cid,title), Enrol(sid,cid): four. Keys sid; (sid,phone); cid; (sid,cid), respectively.

problems.prompt: Does total participation of both entities in Enrol remove the need for an Enrol relation? Explain the distinction between participation and cardinality.
problems.answer: No. Total participation says every entity instance participates at least once; many-to-many cardinality still needs its own relationship relation.

problems.prompt: Customer(email PRIMARY KEY,pid REFERENCES Person) has no other constraints. Does a non-null pid guarantee one customer per person? Can a separate phone column be NULL?
problems.answer: No uniqueness follows for pid. A phone column without NOT NULL or another relevant constraint can be NULL.

teachingSections.title: A schema states rules for every legal table
teachingSections.text: A table’s current rows are one instance. Its schema states the columns and constraints every legal instance must satisfy. Seeing unique values in today’s data does not prove that a column must always be unique. A candidate key is a smallest set of columns guaranteed to identify a row.

teachingSections.title: A foreign key asks for a matching parent
teachingSections.text: Suppose Purchase.pid references Person.pid. A non-null Purchase.pid must match a Person.pid. Several purchase rows can reference the same person. The reference does not make Purchase.pid unique. A primary key must be unique and non-null. Other columns may permit NULL unless another constraint forbids it.

teachingSections.title: Test an operation by looking for a missing reference
teachingSections.text: Adding a parent gives child rows more possible matches. Removing a child removes one reference. Neither operation creates an unmatched reference by itself. Removing a referenced parent or adding a child without a parent can cause a violation. Read any stated cascading behavior before deciding whether the system rejects an operation.

teachingSections.title: Map each independent kind of information
teachingSections.text: An ER model describes entities, their attributes and their relationships. Give each entity a relation. A many-to-many relationship needs a relation containing the participating keys. A multivalued attribute needs a separate relation because one entity can have several values. Total participation means every entity participates at least once. It does not change a many-to-many relationship into a one-to-one relationship.

families.subject: dbms
families.title: Relational algebra and calculus: sets, witnesses and universality
prerequisites: Natural-join matching on all common attributes
families.concept: The central task is translating who qualifies into a set or logical condition while preserving the quantifiers and join attributes.
reasoningSteps: Read the required output attributes.
Translate every operator or quantifier into a condition on a candidate tuple.
Track intermediate relation schemas and duplicate elimination.
Use a witness or missing witness to accept or reject a candidate.
commonFailures: Reading “all” as “some”
Joining only one of several shared columns
Counting witnesses as separate set-projection results
families.workedExample: To require every member of T to occur in A or B, test T−(A∪B)=∅. Using A∩B instead would demand membership in both sets, a stronger requirement.

problems.prompt: T={1,2}, A={1}, B={2}. Evaluate T−(A∪B) and T−(A∩B). Which expresses membership in at least one set?
problems.answer: The differences are ∅ and {1,2}, respectively. The union version expresses at least one.

problems.prompt: X(P,Q)={(1,a),(1,b)} and Y(P,Q,R)={(1,a,9),(1,c,8)}. Compute X natural-join Y and then project P.
problems.answer: Join result {(1,a,9)}, since both P and Q must match. Projection is {1}.

problems.prompt: Enrol(student,course)={(A,x),(A,y),(B,x)} and Required(course)={x,y}. Who is returned by Enrol ÷ Required? State the quantifier explicitly.
problems.answer: A only: for every required course there exists an enrolment pair for that student.

problems.prompt: X(P,Q)={(1,a),(2,b)}; Y(P,S)={(1,4),(1,7),(2,0)}. Select t from X for which there exists m in Y with matching P and S>1. How many result tuples?
problems.answer: One: (1,a). The two witnesses for P=1 do not duplicate t under tuple-calculus set semantics.

problems.prompt: Using the same Enrol relation, add Required course z without adding enrolments. What is the division result? What changes if Required is empty and the candidate students are πstudent(Enrol)?
problems.answer: With z: empty. With no requirements: all candidate students A and B satisfy the universal condition vacuously.

teachingSections.title: Read each operation as a question about rows
teachingSections.text: Selection keeps rows meeting a condition. Projection keeps chosen columns. In ordinary relational algebra, the result is a set, so duplicate projected rows appear only once. A natural join combines rows that agree on every column name the two inputs share. Write the input column names before computing a join.

teachingSections.title: Translate either and every carefully
teachingSections.text: Union collects values appearing in either set. Intersection collects values appearing in both. Set difference T−U keeps values in T that are missing from U. Therefore T−U=∅ means every value in T is present in U. This gives a way to express a requirement by searching for a counterexample to it.

teachingSections.title: An existence test needs one matching witness
teachingSections.text: In tuple relational calculus, a variable can stand for a candidate row. The symbol ∃ means there exists. To test an existence condition, look for at least one row satisfying it. Two matching witnesses still make the same condition true. They do not create two copies of the candidate in a set-valued result.

teachingSections.title: Division asks for complete coverage
teachingSections.text: Suppose Enrol records a student and a course. Dividing by a set of required courses asks which students appear with every required course. Choose a candidate student. Check each required course. One missing course rejects that student. This differs from asking whether the student took at least one required course.

families.subject: dbms
families.title: SQL: aggregation grain, multiplicity and correlated subqueries
families.concept: Correct SQL depends on the unit counted and the row scope of each expression, not just on recognizing COUNT or GROUP BY.
reasoningSteps: State the intended output grain: one row per what?
Materialize groups or matching rows on a tiny instance.
For a correlated subquery, fix one outer row before evaluating its inner query.
Test ties and duplicates explicitly.
commonFailures: Grouping by a unique employee ID when a team size is wanted
Joining a row to itself instead of its whole group
Replacing a strict comparison by a rank formula that mishandles ties
families.workedExample: Employee has rows (e1,T),(e2,T),(e3,U). Grouping by TeamID gives T:2,U:1, but loses per-employee output. Joining these two group counts back on TeamID gives one row per employee with sizes2,2,1.

problems.prompt: For those three employees, what does GROUP BY EmpID with COUNT(*) return? Why is it not the requested team size?
problems.answer: Every employee group contains one row, so all counts are1. The grouping key defines the wrong grain.

problems.prompt: Give a SQL query returning each EmpID and its team size, using a grouped derived table. Assume TeamID is NOT NULL.
problems.answer: SELECT E.EmpID,B.n FROM Employee E JOIN (SELECT TeamID,COUNT(*) AS n FROM Employee GROUP BY TeamID) B ON E.TeamID=B.TeamID;

problems.prompt: Balances are 10,10,20,30. A query keeps an outer row when the count of strictly greater balances is at least the count of strictly smaller balances. Which rows remain? Show greater/smaller counts per distinct value.
problems.answer: 10:greater2,smaller0, so both 10 rows remain. 20:greater1,smaller2, reject. 30:greater0,smaller3, reject. Result has2 rows.

problems.prompt: Loan(branch,amount) rows are (X,40),(X,70),(Y,60),(Y,90). Return rows with amount greater than MAX(amount) over branch X. Is that subquery correlated?
problems.answer: Only (Y,90). The threshold is70 and is independent of the outer row, so the stated subquery is uncorrelated.

problems.prompt: Repeat the balance condition using 5,15,15,15,25. Which rows remain? Explain the role of equality.
problems.answer: 5 has greater4,smaller0 and remains. Each15 has greater1,smaller1 and remains. 25 fails. Four rows remain; equal peers count on neither strict side.

teachingSections.title: Start by saying what one output row should represent
teachingSections.text: A query might need one row per employee or one row per team. Those are different outputs. GROUP BY collects rows sharing the chosen values. Each group produces an aggregate such as COUNT or SUM. Grouping by a unique employee ID creates groups containing only one employee.

teachingSections.title: Compute a team fact, then attach it to each employee
teachingSections.text: To display each employee with their team size, first group by TeamID and count the team’s rows. This produces one result per team. Join those results back to Employee using TeamID. Each employee then receives the count for the correct team. A small team of two employees makes the purpose of each step visible.

teachingSections.title: Decide whether the inner query depends on the outer row
teachingSections.text: A subquery can compute one fixed threshold, such as the largest loan in branch X. Every outer row compares against that same threshold. A correlated subquery instead refers to the current outer row. To evaluate it, fix that outer row first and compute the inner result for that row.

teachingSections.title: Treat equal values explicitly
teachingSections.text: Suppose a condition counts balances strictly greater than the current balance and balances strictly smaller than it. Equal balances belong to neither count. List each distinct balance with its two counts, then apply the condition. If several rows share an accepted balance, each of those rows may appear in an ordinary SQL result. Do not replace the query with an informal ranking shortcut.

families.subject: dbms
families.title: Functional dependencies: closure, minimal keys and decomposition
prerequisites: Applying an FD when all determinant attributes are present
families.concept: A closure is a fixed-point computation. A candidate key also needs minimality, and a decomposition has separate information and constraint properties.
reasoningSteps: Compute closure until no rule adds an attribute.
Find attributes absent from every RHS.
Enumerate minimal determinants rather than stopping after the first key.
Check BCNF for every nontrivial FD; test preservation separately from losslessness.
commonFailures: Applying AB→C when only A is known
Calling a superkey a minimal key
Concluding lossless implies dependency-preserving
families.workedExample: For R(A,B,C,D) with A→B,B→C, every key must include A and D because neither is derivable from another attribute. (AD)+=ABCD and neither A nor D alone is sufficient, so AD is the only candidate key.

problems.prompt: With A→B and BC→D, compute A+ and (AC)+ on R(A,B,C,D).
problems.answer: A+={A,B}; (AC)+={A,B,C,D}. The second rule needs both B and C.

problems.prompt: For R(A,B,C,D), A→B,B→C, find every candidate key and justify mandatory attributes.
problems.answer: Only AD. Both A and D occur on no RHS; together they determine all attributes.

problems.prompt: R(A,B,C,D,E), F={A→BC,CD→E,E→A}. Find every candidate key and explain why no other minimal key exists.
problems.answer: AD,CD,DE. D must occur in every key. With D present, A or E supplies A,B,C,E; C with D supplies E then A,B. Without A,C,E, only B and D are available and closure cannot grow. Each listed pair is minimal.

problems.prompt: R(A,B,C), F={A→B,B→C}, decomposed into AB and AC. Is it lossless? Does it preserve B→C? Give a legal component-instance counterexample for preservation.
problems.answer: Lossless because intersection A determines AB. Not dependency-preserving: AB={(a1,b),(a2,b)}, AC={(a1,c1),(a2,c2)} satisfy projected A→B,A→C but their join violates B→C when c1≠c2.

problems.prompt: R(A,B,C,D), F={A→BC,C→D,B→A}. Find candidate keys and test BCNF.
problems.answer: A and B are candidate keys. C+={C,D}, so nontrivial C→D has a determinant that is not a superkey; BCNF fails.

teachingSections.title: A dependency says what agreement forces
teachingSections.text: The functional dependency A→B says that any two legal rows agreeing on A must also agree on B. It is a rule for all legal data. If the left side contains several attributes, the rows must agree on all of them before the rule applies.

teachingSections.title: Closure collects everything a set determines
teachingSections.text: Start with a set of attributes, such as {A,C}. Add the right side of any dependency whose entire left side is already present. Keep applying rules until nothing new appears. The final set is called the closure, written (AC)+. The plus sign means all attributes that follow from the starting set.

teachingSections.title: A key needs both coverage and minimality
teachingSections.text: A superkey determines every attribute in the relation. A candidate key is a superkey with no unnecessary attributes. Find every candidate key rather than stopping at the first one. An attribute that never appears on a dependency’s right side cannot be obtained from other attributes. Every key must therefore include it.

teachingSections.title: Ask two separate questions about a decomposition
teachingSections.text: A decomposition splits one relation into smaller relations. It is lossless when joining the parts recovers the original information without extra combinations. It preserves dependencies when checking the smaller relations is enough to enforce the original dependency rules. A split can satisfy one property without satisfying the other. BCNF adds another test: every nontrivial dependency must have a superkey on its left side.

families.subject: dbms
families.title: Indexes and B+ trees: access patterns, byte layout and splits
prerequisites: p pointers and p−1 separator keys
families.concept: Index choice follows the query; storage capacity follows a drawn layout; insertion follows the specified separator and split conventions.
reasoningSteps: Separate equality, range and join predicates.
Draw an internal node and account for every field.
Solve a byte inequality and floor at the end.
For insertion, follow the diagram’s separator convention and propagate overflow upward.
commonFailures: Using record-pointer bytes in an internal node
Forgetting the extra child pointer
Applying a familiar separator convention to a different diagram
families.workedExample: If an internal node has p child pointers of8 bytes and p−1 keys of12 bytes, with128 bytes usable and no header, then 8p+12(p−1)≤128. Thus20p≤140 and p≤7. Leaf capacity is a different calculation.

problems.prompt: An internal node has4 child pointers. How many separator keys does it have? Explain with child ranges.
problems.answer: Three separators divide the search space into four child ranges.

problems.prompt: Usable node bytes=256, child pointer=8 bytes, key=16 bytes, no header. Find maximum internal fanout.
problems.answer: 8p+16(p−1)≤256 implies24p≤272, so p=11. Check p=12 exceeds capacity.

problems.prompt: A query filters Category='History' and Rating>4, then joins on IDs. Which filter can an ordinary hash index support directly, and which benefits from an ordered index? Explain without claiming a guaranteed speedup for every dataset.
problems.answer: Hash supports equality on Category; an ordered B+ tree supports the Rating range. Benefit depends on selectivity, layout and the chosen plan; hash does not support ordered range access by itself.

problems.prompt: Leaf capacity2; internal capacity3 children. Separators are minimum keys of right children. Root[5,9] has leaves[1,3],[5,7],[9,11]. Insert2; split a 3-key leaf into a 1-key left and 2-key right leaf; promote the middle separator on internal overflow. Give the new root and its two internal children.
problems.answer: Left leaf splits to[1] and[2,3], adding separator2. Old root becomes[2,5,9] with4 children, so split it and promote5. New root[5], left internal[2], right internal[9].

problems.prompt: Same256-byte internal node as before, but reserve a16-byte header. Recompute fanout and explain whether a12-byte record pointer belongs in the inequality.
problems.answer: 8p+16(p−1)+16≤256 gives24p≤256, so p=10. Record pointers belong to leaves in the stated model, not internal child-pointer slots.

teachingSections.title: An index helps a query find useful rows
teachingSections.text: A hash index organizes keys for exact matching. An ordered index, such as a B+ tree, also supports ranges of keys. Read the query’s conditions first. A condition Category=History asks for equality. Rating>4 asks for a range. Which index helps also depends on how many rows the condition keeps.

teachingSections.title: Internal nodes guide the search
teachingSections.text: A B+ tree has internal nodes that guide the search and leaves that locate the data. If an internal node points to four child ranges, three separator keys divide those ranges. In general, p child pointers go with p−1 keys. The letter p here counts pointers, not bytes.

teachingSections.title: Count the bytes in the node you were asked about
teachingSections.text: Draw the pointer slots and key slots. Multiply the number of each by its byte size. Add any stated header. The total must fit the usable node size. Solve the resulting inequality and choose the largest integer that fits. Data-record pointers used in leaves do not belong in an internal-node calculation unless the question specifies that layout.

teachingSections.title: Insertion can split more than one level
teachingSections.text: First find the leaf where the new key belongs. If it overflows, split it according to the stated rule and add a separator to its parent. The parent can then overflow too. A split reaching the root creates a new root. Read the diagram’s separator convention because textbooks can use different boundary choices.

families.subject: dbms
families.title: Warehouses: hierarchy direction, cuboids and group counts
families.concept: Count choices of aggregation level separately from rows inside a cuboid; drilling down changes resolution rather than filtering an arbitrary subset.
reasoningSteps: State one fact row’s grain.
Name the hierarchy level before and after an operation.
Count cuboids by independent level choices.
For CUBE row counts, sum the sizes of each grouping set.
commonFailures: Confusing the number of cuboids with the number of output rows
Forgetting ALL
Adding averages without group sizes
families.workedExample: For two dimensions with2 and3 observed values and all combinations present, CUBE yields6 detailed groups,2 first-dimension subtotals,3 second-dimension subtotals, and1 grand total:12 rows. There are only4 cuboids (grouping sets).

problems.prompt: A sales cube changes geography from Country to City while preserving Product and Month. Is this roll-up, drill-down, slice or dice? Explain the level change.
problems.answer: Drill-down: geography moves to a more detailed level. It need not select a single city.

problems.prompt: Dimensions Time has Day,Month,Year,ALL and Place has City,Country,ALL. How many cuboids are possible?
problems.answer: 4×3=12 choices of one level per dimension.

problems.prompt: Two dimensions have3 and4 distinct values, with every pair observed. How many cuboids does CUBE(D1,D2) use, and how many output rows?
problems.answer: 4 cuboids; rows12+3+4+1=20. They are different counted objects.

problems.prompt: Only (A,x),(A,y),(B,x) occur in a fact table. How many rows does CUBE(D1,D2) return? Contrast the complete-product shortcut.
problems.answer: 3 detail groups+2 D1 groups+2 D2 groups+1 grand total=8. The complete-product shortcut would incorrectly count a nonexistent (B,y) detail group.

problems.prompt: One subgroup has average sales10 over2 facts; another has average20 over8 facts. Find the combined average and explain the information needed for a roll-up.
problems.answer: (10×2+20×8)/(2+8)=18. Retain sums and counts; the unweighted average15 is wrong.

teachingSections.title: An aggregate describes a chosen level of detail
teachingSections.text: A sales fact might record a product, a day, a city and a quantity. Grouping by month combines several days. Grouping by country combines several cities. A hierarchy lists such levels, for example City→State→Country→ALL. ALL means the total across that dimension.

teachingSections.title: Moving down gives more detail
teachingSections.text: Changing Country to State gives a more detailed view. This operation is called drill-down. Changing State to Country combines detail and is called roll-up. Selecting one country is a different action, often called slicing. Ask what level of detail changes before naming the operation.

teachingSections.title: Count aggregation choices separately from their rows
teachingSections.text: One choice of level for each dimension defines an aggregate view called a cuboid. If Time has four choices including ALL and Place has three, there are4×3=12 cuboids. One cuboid can itself contain many rows. The number of cuboids is therefore different from the number of grouped rows.

teachingSections.title: List the groups produced by CUBE
teachingSections.text: For two columns D1 and D2, CUBE includes detailed groups (D1,D2), D1-only groups, D2-only groups and one grand total. Count the rows in each part. A shortcut based on all possible pairs requires every pair to occur. For averages, keep the subgroup sums and counts so that a later roll-up can weight groups correctly.

families.subject: dbms
families.title: Preprocessing: formulas, reference statistics and information loss
families.concept: A transformation’s name, reference parameters and information-loss assumptions determine what can be computed and what can be recovered.
reasoningSteps: Name the transformation before substituting.
Use only the stated reference statistics.
Keep units and denominator visible.
Check interval endpoints and invertibility separately.
commonFailures: Using a min–max denominator for a z-score
Assuming every transformed value lies in[0,1]
Treating binning as lossless
families.workedExample: For reference mean50 and standard deviation10, a value65 has z-score(65−50)/10=1.5. This says1.5 reference standard deviations above the mean; it is not a percentile or a[0,1] scale.

problems.prompt: Reference mean20, standard deviation4; compute the z-score of26 and interpret its sign.
problems.answer: 1.5; the value is above the reference mean.

problems.prompt: Reference minimum10, maximum30; min–max scale a new value35. Is the result necessarily an error?
problems.answer: (35−10)/(30−10)=1.25. A new input outside the reference range can legitimately map outside[0,1].

problems.prompt: A column has mean80, standard deviation12, min20,max140. Compute both z-score and min–max value for98; identify which statistics each uses.
Bins are[0,10),[10,20),[20,30]. Assign10 and20. Can the original values be recovered from bin labels alone?
problems.answer: 10 enters the second bin;20 enters the third. Exact values cannot in general be recovered.

problems.prompt: Transform x using z=(x−μ)/σ with known σ>0. Can x be recovered? Compare with replacing x by its interval label.
problems.answer: Yes: x=μ+σz if parameters and precision are retained. A bin label usually loses within-bin location. Discretization/compression extensions are syllabus-driven; the direct observed paper anchor here is z-score normalization.

teachingSections.title: A transformation changes how values are represented
teachingSections.text: Suppose two columns use very different units or ranges. Rescaling can make their values easier to compare or use in a model. Different transformations answer different questions. Write the chosen formula before substituting any numbers.

teachingSections.title: A z-score measures distance from the mean
teachingSections.text: Subtract the reference mean from the value. Divide the result by the reference standard deviation. The answer tells you how many reference standard deviations the value lies above or below the mean. A negative answer means below the mean. The standard deviation must be positive for this division.

teachingSections.title: Min–max scaling uses a different reference
teachingSections.text: Subtract the reference minimum. Divide by reference maximum minus reference minimum. Values between those two reference bounds map to0 through1. A later value outside the reference range can map outside0 through1. That result does not by itself show an error. A zero reference range needs separate handling.

teachingSections.title: Some transformations lose detail
teachingSections.text: Binning replaces an exact value with an interval label. Define which bin includes each boundary. Many distinct values can receive the same label, so the label usually cannot recover the original value. By contrast, an exact z-score with known mean and positive standard deviation can be reversed using x=mean+standardDeviation×z. Numerical rounding can still lose precision.
